specStatements.text: The main energy resources available for use on Earth include: fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves.
A renewable energy resource is one that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used.
The uses of energy resources include: transport, electricity generation and heating.
• describe the main energy sources available
• distinguish between energy resources that are renewable and energy resources that are non-renewable
• compare ways that different energy resources are used, the uses to include transport, electricity generation and heating
• understand why some energy resources are more reliable than others
• describe the environmental impact arising from the use of different energy resources
• explain patterns and trends in the use of energy resources.
Descriptions of how energy resources are used to generate electricity are not required.
• consider the environmental issues that may arise from the use of different energy resources

• show that science has the ability to identify environmental issues arising from the use of energy resources but not always the power to deal with the issues because of political, social, ethical or economic considerations.

scopeNotes.statement: Descriptions of how energy resources are used to generate electricity are not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Nothing in this content describes the mechanism by which a resource is turned into electricity. There is no account of boilers, steam, turbines, generators, photovoltaic cells or tidal barrages. Resources are named, classified as renewable or non-renewable, matched to their uses, compared for reliability and judged for environmental impact - which is what the specification asks - but the question 'how does it make the electricity?' is never asked or answered. Where a resource has to be identified, it is identified by where the energy comes from (hot rock, moving air, stored water, sunlight), not by the working of any power station.

scopeNotes.statement: because of political, social, ethical or economic considerations
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The four kinds of consideration are used exactly as the specification names them: political, social, ethical and economic. Content shows that science identifies the environmental issue and that these considerations limit what is actually done about it. It does not teach the detail of any particular government policy, treaty or piece of legislation, and it does not ask students to argue for one political position over another.

concepts.definition: A supply of energy available for people to use. The main energy resources available for use on Earth include fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves. Electricity is not itself an energy resource: it has to be generated using one of these resources.

Fuels formed underground from the remains of living organisms over many millions of years. They are non-renewable: new fossil fuel forms far more slowly than the fuel is being used, so the supply is not replenished as it is used.

Fuel such as uranium, mined from rock and used in nuclear power stations. It is non-renewable, because the supply in the ground is finite and is not replenished as it is used. It releases no carbon dioxide while generating, but it produces radioactive waste.

Fuel made from plant or animal material grown recently, for example wood, or ethanol and biodiesel made from crops. It is renewable, because the crops used to make it can be grown again as the fuel is used. It is burned, so it releases carbon dioxide.

A renewable resource that uses the energy of moving air, mainly to generate electricity. Wind speed changes with the weather, so the output cannot be guaranteed at any particular moment: wind is not a reliable resource.

A renewable resource that uses water held behind a dam, usually in a river valley, to generate electricity. It is replenished by rainfall, and output can normally be supplied when it is wanted, but building the dam floods land.

A renewable resource that uses energy from hot rock beneath the Earth's surface, both for heating and for generating electricity. The rock stays hot day and night in all weathers, so geothermal is reliable, but it is only available in suitable places.

A renewable resource that uses the regular rise and fall of the sea. The tidal cycle repeats predictably each day and does not depend on the weather, so the tides are a reliable resource, although tidal schemes can alter coastal habitats.

A renewable resource. Sunlight is used to generate electricity and also to heat water directly. The energy arriving varies with the time of day, the season and the cloud cover, so the Sun is not a reliable resource on its own.

A renewable resource that uses the movement of waves on the surface of the sea. Wave size depends on the wind, so like wind itself this resource is not reliable. It is a different resource from hydro-electricity and from the tides.
An energy resource that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used. The renewable resources are bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves.
An energy resource that is not replenished as it is used, so the amount available falls as it is used up. The non-renewable resources are the fossil fuels - coal, oil and gas - and nuclear fuel.

Moving people and goods. Most transport runs on fuels refined from oil - petrol, diesel and aviation fuel. Bio-fuel is used in some vehicles, nuclear fuel powers some ships and submarines, and electricity is used in electric vehicles and trains.

Producing electricity for homes and industry. Almost every resource can be used for this: fossil fuels, nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves. How each resource is used to generate the electricity is not required.
Warming buildings and water. This is done mainly by burning gas, oil or wood (a bio-fuel), and in some places by using geothermal energy, by solar heating of water, or by electricity.

A reliable energy resource is one that can supply energy whenever it is needed. Fossil fuels, nuclear fuel and bio-fuel can be burned on demand; geothermal is always available and the tides follow a predictable cycle, so these are reliable. Wind, the Sun and water waves depend on conditions that change from hour to hour, and hydro-electricity depends on rainfall, so these are less reliable.

The harm done to the environment by obtaining and using an energy resource. Every resource has some impact: renewable does not mean harmless. Impacts include gases released into the atmosphere, waste that must be stored, land taken or flooded, habitats damaged, and noise and visual intrusion.

concepts.term: Carbon dioxide released by burning fuels
concepts.definition: Burning fossil fuels and bio-fuels releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Increasing the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere contributes to global warming and climate change. Nuclear fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves do not release carbon dioxide as they are used.

Coal and oil contain sulfur impurities. When they are burned, sulfur dioxide is released, and this contributes to acid rain, which damages trees, soils, lakes and buildings. Carbon dioxide does not cause acid rain.

Using nuclear fuel produces waste that remains radioactive and dangerous for a very long time, so it must be stored securely. There is also the risk, however small, of an accident releasing radioactive material.

concepts.term: Impact on land, habitats and views
concepts.definition: Renewable schemes take up space and change places. Hydro-electric dams flood valleys and destroy habitats, tidal schemes alter estuaries and the wildlife living there, wind farms are noisy and are objected to as a spoiling of the view, and growing crops for bio-fuel uses land that could grow food and can clear natural habitat.

concepts.term: Patterns and trends in the use of energy resources
concepts.definition: Over recent decades the share of energy supplied by renewable resources has grown and the share supplied by coal has fallen, driven by concern about climate change, by government targets and by the falling cost of renewable schemes. Change is slow because new schemes are expensive and take years to build, because existing vehicles, boilers and power stations were built for fossil fuels, and because some renewables are less reliable.

concepts.term: Political, social, ethical and economic considerations
concepts.definition: Science can identify an environmental issue caused by using an energy resource, but it does not by itself have the power to deal with it. What is actually done depends on political decisions, on what people are willing to accept, on ethical judgements about fairness to other countries and to future generations, and on the economic cost of change and the jobs and industries involved.

misconceptions.question: Does 'renewable' mean a resource can never run out?
misconceptions.correct: A renewable resource is one that is being, or can be, replenished as it is used.
misconceptions.misconception: Renewable means there is an unlimited supply, so you can use as much as you like and it will never run out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday sense of 'renewable' suggests endlessness, and students meet the word alongside phrases like 'the wind will always blow'. The definition is about replacement keeping pace with use, not about an infinite store.
misconceptions.correction: Focus on the specification's wording: the resource is being replenished as it is used. Bio-fuel is renewable only because crops are grown again; if they were not replanted it would run out. The test is replacement, not size of supply.

misconceptions.question: Is nuclear fuel renewable because it releases no carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: Nuclear fuel is non-renewable. It releases no carbon dioxide when generating, but the uranium is not replenished as it is used.
misconceptions.misconception: Nuclear fuel must be renewable, because renewables are the clean ones and nuclear does not give off carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students merge two separate ideas - 'renewable' and 'low-carbon' - into a single category of 'good' resources, because the two usually go together for wind, solar and tidal.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the two questions apart. Is it replenished as it is used? That decides renewable or non-renewable. Does it release carbon dioxide? That is a separate environmental question. Nuclear fuel answers no to both.

misconceptions.question: Is bio-fuel non-renewable because burning it releases carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: Bio-fuel is renewable, because the plants used to make it can be grown again as it is used.
misconceptions.misconception: Bio-fuel gets burned and gives off carbon dioxide just like coal, so it must be a non-renewable fuel too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students classify by what happens at the point of use - burning and smoke - rather than by whether the supply is replaced. Bio-fuel behaves like a fossil fuel in a burner, so it gets filed with them.
misconceptions.correction: Classify by replenishment. A crop grown this year and burned this year is replaced by next year's crop, so bio-fuel is renewable. Coal took millions of years to form and is not being replaced at the rate it is used.

misconceptions.question: Do renewable energy resources have no environmental impact?
misconceptions.correct: Every energy resource has some environmental impact; renewable does not mean harmless.
misconceptions.misconception: Renewables are the clean, green option, so using them does no damage to the environment at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Renewables are presented as the answer to the problems caused by fossil fuels, and the contrast is often drawn so sharply that students hear 'no impact' rather than 'less of one particular impact'.
misconceptions.correction: Name a specific impact for each renewable: hydro-electric dams flood valleys and destroy habitats, tidal schemes alter estuaries, wind farms bring noise and visual intrusion, bio-fuel crops take land that could grow food and release carbon dioxide when burned.

misconceptions.question: Is wind a reliable energy resource because it is always windy somewhere?
misconceptions.correct: Wind is not reliable, because the wind speed at a wind farm changes with the weather and can fall to nothing.
misconceptions.misconception: The wind never stops completely, so wind is a reliable resource that can be counted on at any time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason from the whole planet rather than from the site of the wind farm, and from 'the resource still exists' rather than 'the energy is available here, now, in the amount needed'.
misconceptions.correction: Reliability means energy is available when it is wanted. A still, cold, windless evening is exactly when demand is high and a wind farm delivers least. That is why wind is classed as unreliable.

misconceptions.question: Are the tides unreliable because they depend on the weather?
misconceptions.correct: The tides follow a regular, predictable cycle that does not depend on the weather, so they are a reliable resource.
misconceptions.misconception: The tides are part of the sea, and the sea is controlled by the weather, so tidal energy is as unpredictable as wind or waves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Tides, waves and wind all get grouped as 'natural, outdoor, weather things'. Students do not separate the daily tidal rhythm from the state of the sea surface.
misconceptions.correction: Separate tides from waves. Tide tables are printed years in advance because the cycle is predictable; wave height cannot be printed years ahead because it depends on the wind. Tides are reliable, waves are not.

misconceptions.question: Are hydro-electricity and water waves the same energy resource?
misconceptions.correct: They are separate resources. Hydro-electricity uses water held behind a dam; water waves use the movement of waves on the sea surface.
misconceptions.misconception: They both use water, so hydro-electricity and wave energy are two names for the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The specification lists both, and both are named after water, so students collapse them into one category and then cannot list nine separate resources.
misconceptions.correction: Sort by where the energy comes from: hydro-electricity from water stored high up behind a dam, water waves from the moving surface of the sea, the tides from the daily rise and fall of sea level. Three different entries in the list.

misconceptions.question: Does geothermal energy come from the Sun warming the ground?
misconceptions.correct: Geothermal energy comes from hot rock beneath the Earth's surface.
misconceptions.misconception: The ground is warm because the Sun has been shining on it, so geothermal energy is really just stored solar energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students' direct experience of warm ground is a sunny day, and the everyday explanation for anything warm outdoors is the Sun.
misconceptions.correction: Geothermal schemes drill deep into rock that is hot day and night, in winter as well as summer, and in places where the surface is under snow. That is why geothermal is reliable and solar is not.

misconceptions.question: Are fossil fuels used only to generate electricity?
misconceptions.correct: Fossil fuels are used for all three uses: transport, electricity generation and heating.
misconceptions.misconception: Fossil fuels are the power station fuels, so if we stopped generating electricity from them we would have stopped using them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy resources are usually first met in the context of power stations, so 'fossil fuel' becomes tied to that single use in students' minds.
misconceptions.correction: Track oil in particular: petrol and diesel for road transport, aviation fuel for aircraft, oil and gas burned in boilers for heating, as well as gas burned in power stations. One resource, three uses.

misconceptions.question: Does an electric car use no energy resource?
misconceptions.correct: An electric car uses whichever resources generated the electricity it was charged with.
misconceptions.misconception: Electric cars run on electricity rather than fuel, so they use no energy resource and cause no environmental impact.
misconceptions.whyItArises: There is no exhaust pipe and nothing is burned in the vehicle, so the environmental impact is invisible to the user. Students treat electricity as a resource in its own right.
misconceptions.correction: Electricity is not an energy resource: it has to be generated from one. If the electricity came from a coal station, carbon dioxide was released; if it came from wind, very little was. The impact moves, it does not disappear.

misconceptions.question: Is carbon dioxide the gas that causes acid rain?
misconceptions.correct: Sulfur dioxide, released when fuels containing sulfur are burned, contributes to acid rain. Carbon dioxide contributes to global warming.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon dioxide is the pollutant from burning fuels, so it must be behind acid rain as well as everything else.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon dioxide is the one gas from burning that students can name confidently, so it gets attached to every environmental problem they meet.
misconceptions.correction: Pair each gas with its own problem: carbon dioxide with global warming and climate change, sulfur dioxide with acid rain. Coal and oil contain sulfur impurities; that is where the sulfur dioxide comes from.

misconceptions.question: Do nuclear power stations release large amounts of carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: Nuclear fuel releases no carbon dioxide while generating. Its main environmental impact is radioactive waste that stays dangerous for a long time.
misconceptions.misconception: Nuclear power stations have those huge towers with clouds pouring out of them, so they must be pumping out carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cooling towers releasing water vapour look exactly like the pictures used to illustrate pollution, and 'nuclear' already carries a strong sense of danger, so the two are merged.
misconceptions.correction: Match each resource to its own impact. Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide and, for coal and oil, sulfur dioxide. Nuclear fuel releases neither, but leaves radioactive waste needing secure storage for a very long time.

misconceptions.question: If science identifies an environmental problem, can science always solve it?
misconceptions.correct: Science can identify environmental issues arising from the use of energy resources, but it does not always have the power to deal with them.
misconceptions.misconception: Scientists have worked out what the problem is, so they will fix it; it is just a matter of time before the technology arrives.
misconceptions.whyItArises: School science shows problems being solved, so students expect an answer to follow every problem. The distinction between knowing what is wrong and being able to act on it is not obvious.
misconceptions.correction: Identifying an issue and dealing with it are different things. What is actually done depends on political decisions, on what society will accept, on ethical judgements and on economic cost - and none of those is settled in a laboratory.

misconceptions.question: Does 'reliable' mean the resource supplies a lot of energy?
misconceptions.correct: Reliable means the resource can supply energy whenever it is needed, not that it supplies a large amount.
misconceptions.misconception: A reliable energy resource is a powerful one - the ones that give out the most energy are the reliable ones.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Reliable', 'powerful' and 'good' merge into one vague idea of quality, and students have no separate slot for availability on demand.
misconceptions.correction: Test with a question: can it deliver at three in the morning in December? Geothermal and gas can, so they are reliable. Solar cannot, whatever the size of the array, so it is not.

misconceptions.question: Is nuclear fuel a type of fossil fuel because it is mined?
misconceptions.correct: Nuclear fuel is a separate resource from the fossil fuels. The fossil fuels are coal, oil and gas.
misconceptions.misconception: Uranium is dug out of the ground like coal, so nuclear fuel belongs with the fossil fuels.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students use 'comes out of the ground' as the defining feature of a fossil fuel, instead of 'formed from the remains of organisms'. Both being non-renewable strengthens the link.
misconceptions.correction: Fossil fuels formed from the remains of living organisms and are burned. Uranium is a metal from rock and is not burned. They share only the label non-renewable.

misconceptions.question: Are fossil fuels renewable because more is still forming underground?
misconceptions.correct: Fossil fuels are non-renewable, because they are not being replenished at anything like the rate at which they are used.
misconceptions.misconception: New coal and oil are still forming below the ground, so fossil fuels are being replenished and count as renewable.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The definition says 'being replenished', and it is true that the process has not stopped. Students apply the definition without weighing the rate against the rate of use.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the timescales. Fossil fuels take millions of years to form; the world burns them in decades. Replenishment that slow is no replenishment at all in practice, so they are non-renewable.

misconceptions.question: Do solar resources supply nothing except on bright summer days?
misconceptions.correct: Solar output falls when it is cloudy, in winter and at night, but is not zero whenever the Sun is not shining brightly. The point is that output cannot be relied on.
misconceptions.misconception: Solar panels only work in strong sunshine, so in a cloudy country they simply do not work.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reliability argument is remembered as a blunt 'solar does not work here', which is an overcorrection of a fair point about variable output.
misconceptions.correction: State the argument precisely: output varies with time of day, season and cloud, so the supply cannot be guaranteed when it is wanted. That is why solar is classed as unreliable, not because it produces nothing.

misconceptions.question: Are renewables always the cheapest choice, so we only still use fossil fuels out of ignorance?
misconceptions.correct: Change is slowed by economic, political, social and ethical considerations, not by lack of scientific knowledge.
misconceptions.misconception: Everyone knows renewables are cheaper and better, so continuing with fossil fuels can only be stupidity or people not believing the science.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The scientific case for reducing fossil fuel use is clear, so students assume that anything preventing change must be a failure to understand it.
misconceptions.correction: Set out the real obstacles: new schemes cost a great deal up front and take years to build, existing vehicles, boilers and power stations were designed for fossil fuels, jobs and industries depend on them, and some renewables are less reliable.

misconceptions.question: Is bio-fuel harmless to the environment because it is renewable?
misconceptions.correct: Bio-fuel releases carbon dioxide when burned, and growing the crops takes land that could grow food or support wildlife.
misconceptions.misconception: Bio-fuel is grown from plants and is renewable, so using it does no environmental damage.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 'bio' prefix and the idea of a growing crop signal natural and safe, and the fact that the fuel is still burned is easily overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: Bio-fuel is burned like any other fuel, so carbon dioxide is released. Add the land-use impact: crops grown for fuel occupy ground that could feed people, and natural habitat is sometimes cleared to grow them.

misconceptions.question: Is heating just a part of electricity generation rather than a separate use?
misconceptions.correct: Heating is one of the three uses named in the specification, alongside transport and electricity generation.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating happens by plugging things in, so heating is really just another way of using electricity, not a use of energy resources in its own right.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet electric heaters and kettles, and do not connect the gas boiler or wood burner with the same list of energy resources.
misconceptions.correction: Most heating of buildings burns gas, oil or wood directly - no electricity involved. Geothermal energy and solar water heating also heat directly. Heating is its own use, and different resources suit it.

misconceptions.question: Are bio-fuel and fossil fuel the same kind of resource?
misconceptions.correct: They are different resources. Bio-fuel is renewable; fossil fuels are non-renewable.
misconceptions.misconception: Both came from living things and both get burned, so bio-fuel and coal must belong to the same group.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The origin story of fossil fuels - formed from the remains of organisms - sounds like the origin of bio-fuel, and both are combusted.
misconceptions.correction: The difference is time and replacement. Bio-fuel comes from a crop grown this year that can be grown again; coal comes from organisms that lived millions of years ago and is not being replaced as it is used.

misconceptions.question: Have renewables already replaced fossil fuels?
misconceptions.correct: The share supplied by renewables is rising, but fossil fuels still supply a large part of the world's energy.
misconceptions.misconception: Wind and solar have taken over now, so fossil fuels are basically finished as a source of energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: News coverage highlights records and milestones for renewable generation, and students generalise a growing share into a completed replacement.
misconceptions.correction: Read trends carefully: a rising share is not a finished change. Transport and heating in particular still run largely on oil and gas, and the change is limited by cost, existing equipment and reliability.

misconceptions.question: Can every energy resource be used for every purpose?
misconceptions.correct: Resources differ in what they suit. Some serve all three uses; others are only practical for one or two.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy is energy, so any resource on the list could be used for transport, for heating or for generating electricity, whichever we chose.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Comparing resources by a single measure - renewable or not, clean or not - hides the fact that they are used in different ways and in different places.
misconceptions.correction: Compare use by use. Bio-fuel serves transport, generation and heating. Water waves and the tides realistically serve generation only. Oil dominates transport. Geothermal heats and generates, but only where the hot rock is.

misconceptions.question: Is the Sun only used to generate electricity?
misconceptions.correct: The Sun is used to generate electricity and also to heat water directly, which is a heating use rather than generation.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything solar on a roof is a solar panel making electricity, so the Sun's only use is electricity generation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Solar electricity is the version students see in the news, and both kinds of panel look similar from the ground.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish the two uses. Solar water heating warms water for the building directly - no electricity is generated at any point. Sort solar examples by the use they serve, not by the fact that they are on a roof.

misconceptions.question: Does 'unreliable' mean the equipment keeps breaking down?
misconceptions.correct: Unreliable here means the supply of energy cannot be guaranteed when it is needed, because the resource itself varies.
misconceptions.misconception: Wind and solar are called unreliable because the turbines and panels are badly built and go wrong a lot.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday language an unreliable machine is a faulty one, and students carry that meaning across without noticing that the term describes the resource, not the hardware.
misconceptions.correction: The word describes availability of the resource. A wind turbine in perfect working order produces nothing on a still day. That is the sense in which wind is unreliable.

misconceptions.question: Is a resource unreliable if it damages the environment?
misconceptions.correct: Reliability and environmental impact are separate judgements. A resource can be reliable and damaging, or clean and unreliable.
misconceptions.misconception: Coal is bad for the environment, so it must be one of the unreliable resources; wind is clean, so it must be reliable.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students sort resources onto a single good-bad scale, so every favourable word attaches to one group and every unfavourable word to the other.
misconceptions.correction: Judge each resource twice, on two separate questions. Coal is reliable but damaging. Wind is much cleaner but unreliable. Geothermal happens to be both reliable and clean - but that has to be shown, not assumed.

misconceptions.question: Does taking energy from the wind use the wind up?
misconceptions.correct: Wind is renewable: it is continually replenished, so using it does not exhaust the supply.
misconceptions.misconception: If turbines take energy out of the wind, then over time there will be less wind, so wind is being used up like a fuel.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students apply the fuel model - a store that empties - to every resource, and the definition of renewable is not yet doing the work of distinguishing a store from a flow.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the definition: is it being replenished as it is used? Wind is continually replenished, so it is renewable. Compare with coal, which is a store built up over millions of years and not replaced as it is burned.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly classifies nuclear fuel and gives the correct reason?

options.text: Renewable, because generating with it does not release any carbon dioxide
options.rationale: The claim about carbon dioxide is true, but it is an environmental point, not the renewable test. Students who treat 'clean' and 'renewable' as one category pick this.

options.text: Non-renewable, because nuclear fuel is one of the fossil fuels found in rock
options.rationale: Reaches the right label by the wrong route: uranium is mined, so students file it with coal. Fossil fuels are only coal, oil and gas.

options.text: Renewable, because a small mass of fuel lasts for a very long time indeed
options.rationale: Treats renewable as meaning 'a supply that will not run out soon'. Size of supply is not the test; replenishment is.

options.text: Non-renewable, because the uranium used is not replenished as it is used
options.rationale: Classification follows the specification's test: a renewable resource is one being, or able to be, replenished as it is used. Uranium in the ground is not, so nuclear fuel is non-renewable.

mcqs.stem: Which group contains only renewable energy resources?

options.text: Bio-fuel, geothermal and water waves
options.rationale: All three are replenished as they are used: crops are regrown, the rock stays hot, and waves keep forming.

options.text: Nuclear fuel, geothermal and the tides
options.rationale: Nuclear fuel is non-renewable. Students who group it with the low-carbon resources include it here.

options.text: Bio-fuel, water waves and natural gas
options.rationale: Natural gas is a fossil fuel. Students who know gas is still forming underground count it as replenished.

options.text: Coal, bio-fuel and hydro-electricity
options.rationale: Coal is non-renewable. Students who treat coal and bio-fuel as the same sort of burnable plant material include both.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is the correct definition of a renewable energy resource?

options.text: One that will never run out, however quickly it is used up
options.rationale: The everyday reading of 'renewable' as endless. It ignores the need for replacement to keep pace.

options.text: One that gives out no carbon dioxide at all when it is used
options.rationale: Confuses the renewable test with an environmental one. Bio-fuel is renewable yet releases carbon dioxide.

options.text: One that is being, or can be, replenished as it is used
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition exactly: replenishment keeping pace with use.

options.text: One that supplies energy at a steady rate whenever needed
options.rationale: Confuses renewable with reliable. Wind is renewable but not reliable; gas is reliable but not renewable.

mcqs.stem: Why is bio-fuel classified as a renewable energy resource?

options.text: Because burning bio-fuel causes no environmental damage at all
options.rationale: The 'bio' label suggests harmlessness, but the fuel is still burned and the crops still take land.

options.text: Because burning bio-fuel releases no carbon dioxide into the air
options.rationale: Factually wrong - bio-fuel is burned and releases carbon dioxide. Chosen by students who equate renewable with carbon-free.

options.text: Because the plants used to make it are grown again as it is used
options.rationale: This is the specification's test applied directly: the resource is replenished as it is used.

options.text: Because the world's supply of bio-fuel can never be used up
options.rationale: Renewable read as inexhaustible. If crops were not replanted, bio-fuel would run out.

mcqs.stem: New coal is still forming underground today. Why is coal still classed as non-renewable?

options.text: Non-renewable resources are the ones that give off polluting gases
options.rationale: Uses pollution as the classifier. Bio-fuel gives off carbon dioxide yet is renewable, so this cannot be the test.

options.text: It forms far more slowly than it is used, so it is not replenished
options.rationale: The test is whether replacement keeps pace with use. Coal forms over millions of years and is burned in decades.

options.text: Non-renewable resources are the ones that supply energy reliably
options.rationale: Confuses reliability with renewability. The tides are reliable and renewable, so the two are not linked.

options.text: It is being replenished, so it should really be classed as renewable
options.rationale: Applies the definition without checking the rate. Formation continuing is not replenishment as it is used.

mcqs.stem: Which one of these energy resources is non-renewable?

options.text: Hydro-electricity, using water held behind a dam
options.rationale: Renewable, replenished by rainfall. Picked by students who confuse it with a fuel that is used up.

options.text: Bio-fuel, made from crops that are grown for burning
options.rationale: Renewable, because the crops are regrown. Chosen by students who classify it by the burning.

options.text: Geothermal, using heat from rock under the surface
options.rationale: Renewable and reliable. Picked by students who think the rock will cool down and be used up.

options.text: Nuclear fuel, from uranium that is mined from rock
options.rationale: The uranium in the ground is finite and is not replenished as it is used, so nuclear fuel is non-renewable.

mcqs.stem: Which energy resource supplies most of the energy used for transport worldwide?

options.text: Oil, which is refined into petrol, diesel and aviation fuel
options.rationale: Transport runs overwhelmingly on fuels refined from oil, which is why transport is the hardest use to move away from fossil fuels.

options.text: Coal, which is burned in the engines of most road vehicles
options.rationale: Coal is associated with fuel and with power stations, but road vehicles run on oil products, not coal.

options.text: Electricity, because all vehicles now run on rechargeable batteries
options.rationale: Electricity is not an energy resource at all - it has to be generated - and most vehicles are not electric.

options.text: Natural gas, which is piped straight to filling stations for cars
options.rationale: Assumes any fuel can serve any use. Gas is used mainly for heating and generation, not for road transport.

mcqs.stem: A house is heated by burning natural gas in a boiler. Which statement about this is correct?

options.text: Gas is only ever used to generate electricity, never for heating
options.rationale: Ties gas to power stations alone. Heating is one of the three named uses, and gas is the main resource used for it.

options.text: Gas is a non-renewable fossil fuel, used here for heating
options.rationale: Correctly names the resource type and the use. Heating is a use of energy resources in its own right, separate from generation.

options.text: Gas is renewable, because new gas keeps forming under the sea
options.rationale: Formation continues, but far too slowly to replace what is used, so gas is non-renewable.

options.text: Gas is renewable, because it burns more cleanly than coal does
options.rationale: Cleanliness is an environmental judgement, not the renewable test. Gas is a fossil fuel and non-renewable.

mcqs.stem: Which resource can be used for all three of transport, electricity generation and heating?

options.text: Water waves, which can drive vehicles as well as power stations
options.rationale: Assumes resources are interchangeable. Wave energy is realistically used for electricity generation only.

options.text: Bio-fuel, which is burned in vehicles, power stations and boilers
options.rationale: Bio-fuel serves all three named uses: it drives vehicles, generates electricity and heats buildings when burned as wood.

options.text: Geothermal, which is used in vehicles and in power stations
options.rationale: Geothermal does heat and generate, but only where hot rock is accessible, and it does not power vehicles.

options.text: The tides, which are used in vehicles and to heat buildings
options.rationale: Again treats every resource as usable for every purpose. Tidal energy is used for electricity generation.

mcqs.stem: Solar panels on a roof warm water for a house. Which use of energy resources is this?

options.text: Electricity generation, since solar panels always make electricity
options.rationale: Assumes every roof panel is photovoltaic. Solar water heating warms the water directly, generating nothing.

options.text: Electricity generation, since the hot water later drives a turbine
options.rationale: Imports a power-station picture into a domestic system. The hot water is used in the house, not to generate.

options.text: Neither, because sunlight in the UK is far too weak to heat water
options.rationale: Overstates the reliability point into 'solar does not work'. Output varies; it is not absent.

options.text: Heating, because energy from the Sun warms the water directly
options.rationale: The Sun is being used for heating, one of the three named uses; no electricity is produced at any stage.

mcqs.stem: Why is a wind farm a less reliable energy resource than a gas-fired power station?

options.text: Wind turbines break down far more often than a gas power station
options.rationale: Reads 'unreliable' as 'faulty equipment'. The term describes availability of the resource, not the hardware.

options.text: Each turbine transfers much less energy than a gas power station
options.rationale: Confuses reliability with amount of energy supplied. A larger wind farm would still stop on a still day.

options.text: The wind does not always blow, so output cannot be guaranteed
options.rationale: Reliability means energy is available when it is wanted. Wind speed varies with the weather, so it cannot be guaranteed.

options.text: Wind farms do more damage to the environment than gas stations
options.rationale: Answers about environmental impact instead of reliability, and the claim itself is wrong for carbon dioxide.

mcqs.stem: Tidal energy is described as a reliable resource. Which statement explains why?

options.text: The tides transfer far more energy than any other resource
options.rationale: Treats reliable as meaning powerful. The size of the supply says nothing about when it is available.

options.text: Tidal equipment is stronger, so it hardly ever breaks down
options.rationale: Reads reliability as freedom from breakdowns rather than as a property of the resource itself.

options.text: The tides depend on the weather, which is easy to forecast
options.rationale: Groups tides with waves and wind as weather-driven. Tides follow their own cycle, independent of the weather.

options.text: The tides rise and fall in a regular, predictable daily cycle
options.rationale: Because the cycle repeats predictably and does not depend on the weather, the supply can be counted on in advance.

mcqs.stem: A country needs electricity at all hours, in any weather. Which resources suit that best?

options.text: Nuclear fuel and gas, because their output can be controlled
options.rationale: Both can supply energy on demand whatever the weather, which is exactly what reliability means.

options.text: Wind and water waves, because there is always some wind
options.rationale: Reasons from 'it is windy somewhere' rather than from output at this site now. Both depend on the weather.

options.text: Solar only, because sunlight reaches the ground each day
options.rationale: Sunlight does arrive daily, but not at night and not evenly, so output cannot be guaranteed.

options.text: Solar and wind, because renewables are the best resources
options.rationale: Sorts resources on a single good-bad scale. Low environmental impact does not make a resource reliable.

mcqs.stem: Which environmental impact arises mainly from burning fossil fuels?

options.text: Carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere as the fuel burns
options.rationale: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, and the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide contributes to climate change.

options.text: Radioactive waste that has to be stored safely for many years
options.rationale: This is the impact of nuclear fuel, not of burning fossil fuels. Chosen when impacts are not matched to resources.

options.text: Loss of habitat when a river valley is flooded behind a dam
options.rationale: A real environmental impact, but of hydro-electricity. Students who recall impacts as a list may attach any one to any resource.

options.text: No impact at all, provided that the fuel is burned efficiently
options.rationale: Efficient burning still releases carbon dioxide. Selected by students who think impact depends on how well a fuel is used.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an environmental impact of burning coal in a power station?

options.text: Release of radioactive waste that must be stored for years
options.rationale: Radioactive waste comes from nuclear fuel. Any large power station with cooling towers can look the same to students.

options.text: Release of carbon dioxide, which then falls as acid rain
options.rationale: Coal does release carbon dioxide, but carbon dioxide is linked to global warming, not to acid rain.

options.text: No impact, because coal is a natural material from the ground
options.rationale: Treats 'natural' as meaning harmless. Where a fuel comes from says nothing about what burning it releases.

options.text: Release of sulfur dioxide, which contributes to acid rain
options.rationale: Coal contains sulfur impurities, so burning it releases sulfur dioxide, and this contributes to acid rain.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the environmental impact of renewable resources is correct?

options.text: Renewable resources have no environmental impact of any kind
options.rationale: The clean-versus-dirty contrast is heard as 'no impact'. Every resource changes the environment in some way.

options.text: Growing crops for bio-fuel has no effect on land or wildlife
options.rationale: Bio-fuel crops occupy land that could grow food, and habitat is sometimes cleared to plant them.

options.text: Hydro-electric schemes can flood valleys and destroy habitats
options.rationale: Damming a valley covers land with water, which destroys the habitats there. Renewable does not mean harmless.

options.text: Using wind uses the wind up, so there will be less wind later
options.rationale: Applies the model of a fuel store emptying to a resource that is continually replenished.

mcqs.stem: Which environmental impact is associated with the use of nuclear fuel?

options.text: Large amounts of carbon dioxide released while generating
options.rationale: Cooling towers releasing water vapour look like pollution, but nuclear generation releases no carbon dioxide.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide released, which then causes acid rain to form
options.rationale: Sulfur dioxide comes from burning coal and oil. Nothing is burned in a nuclear power station.

options.text: Radioactive waste that stays dangerous for a very long time
options.rationale: This is the characteristic impact of nuclear fuel: waste that remains radioactive and must be stored securely.

options.text: None, because nuclear fuel is a very concentrated energy source
options.rationale: A small mass of fuel does supply a great deal of energy, but that does not remove the waste problem.

mcqs.stem: The share of UK electricity generated from renewables has risen sharply. Why?

options.text: Concern about climate change has driven investment in renewables
options.rationale: The environmental impact of burning fossil fuels, together with government targets and falling costs, explains the trend.

options.text: Renewable schemes have always been the cheapest option there is
options.rationale: Costs have fallen, but renewable schemes were expensive for years and were still built, so cost alone is not the reason.

options.text: Fossil fuels ran out completely, so nothing else was left to use
options.rationale: Fossil fuels have not run out; they still supply a large share of energy, especially for transport and heating.

options.text: Renewable resources became reliable enough to be used on their own
options.rationale: Wind and solar output still varies with the weather, which is why other resources are still needed alongside them.

mcqs.stem: Fossil fuels still supply much of the world's energy. Why is the change away so slow?

options.text: Renewable resources have already replaced them almost everywhere
options.rationale: Confuses a rising share with a completed change. Transport and heating still run largely on oil and gas.

options.text: Building new schemes costs a great deal and takes many years
options.rationale: Economic cost, the time to build, and equipment already designed for fossil fuels all slow the change down.

options.text: Scientists do not agree that fossil fuels harm the environment
options.rationale: The scientific case is not the obstacle. Science identifies the issue; other considerations limit what is done.

options.text: Fossil fuels are renewable, so there is no reason to change now
options.rationale: Fossil fuels are not replenished at the rate they are used, so they are non-renewable.

mcqs.stem: Scientists identified the harm caused by burning fossil fuels, yet their use goes on. Why?

options.text: Science can always solve a problem once it has identified it
options.rationale: Identifying an issue and being able to deal with it are different. Science does not always have the power to act.

options.text: Political, social, ethical and economic factors limit what is done
options.rationale: This is the specification's point: science identifies the issue but these considerations govern what is actually done.

options.text: The evidence for the harm is not accepted by most scientists
options.rationale: Assumes the obstacle must be scientific doubt. The science identified the issue; the barriers lie elsewhere.

options.text: Governments have in fact already stopped all fossil fuel use
options.rationale: Contradicts the stem and the trend data. Use has not stopped; the share supplied by renewables has grown.
